questions.scenario: 20,000 finished tees (cost ৳400/pc) sit in the FG warehouse, unsold. On today's Balance Sheet they are:
options: An expense — production cost must be expensed immediately
An asset (Inventory—FG ৳80,00,000) until ownership passes to the buyer
Revenue already, since they're complete
A liability to the workers who made them
questions.explanation: Unsold goods are money in another form — an asset. The expense (COGS) waits for the sale event. Expensing production immediately is the March/April lie from this module's mystery.
wrongExplanations: That breaks matching: expense belongs with the SALE of the same units.
Completeness isn't a sale; ownership transfer on the B/L date is.
Worker obligations were recorded when wages accrued — unrelated to the shirts' classification.

questions.scenario: For Masco's exports, inventory becomes COGS exactly when:
options: Production finishes and QC passes
The B/L is issued and invoice raised (ownership passes)
H&M's cash lands in City Bank
Year-end arrives
questions.explanation: The B/L date is both revenue recognition AND COGS trigger — R4 and R5 fire together, keeping revenue and cost matched to the same physical shipment.
wrongExplanations: Finished ≠ sold; it just moved from WIP to FG asset.
Cash collection merely converts receivable to bank — profit was earned at the B/L date, not then.
Calendar dates don't move ownership; shipping documents do.

questions.scenario: March: heavy production, few shipments. April: Eid pause, heavy shipments. Someone expensed all production monthly. Result?
options: Both months reported honestly
March looked artificially profitable, April artificially loss-making — opposite lies from breaking matching
Both months showed losses
No financial impact at all
questions.explanation: March pushed its costs into 'expense' while earning nothing; April then shipped units whose costs had ALREADY been expensed once — so April's costs double-hit. Correct inventory accounting makes both months truthful.
wrongExplanations: That's precisely the disease this module exists to cure.
April actually gets hit TWICE under this error, not zero or balanced times.
Misclassification always distorts — that's why auditors hunt it.

questions.scenario: PO-2291 ships: invoice ৳1,10,00,000; true accumulated cost ৳80,00,000. Which entries fire together on B/L date?
options: Only Dr AR / Cr Revenue
Only Dr COGS / Cr Inventory
R4: Dr AR 1.10Cr / Cr Revenue 1.10Cr AND R5: Dr COGS 80L / Cr Inventory—FG 80L — atomically
Dr Cash / Cr Revenue now, COGS later when convenient
questions.explanation: One shipment event = matched pair of entries written atomically by the posting engine. Gross profit (30L, 27%) emerges honestly for those exact units.
wrongExplanations: Revenue without COGS overstates profit by the entire product cost.
COGS without revenue understates it — and orphans the cost from any sale.
'Convenient' timing = unmatched books = audit findings.

questions.scenario: Yarn arrived at ৳600/kg in January and ৳640/kg in June. August fabric consumes yarn. Which costing does our ERP use for the consumption price?
options: LIFO — newest first
Moving weighted average — all layers blended into one fair average updated at each arrival
Whatever rate makes profit look best that month
January's rate forever
questions.explanation: Continuous processes suit moving weighted average: smooth, fair, hard to game, IFRS-compliant. LIFO is prohibited under IFRS; cherry-picking rates is fraud territory.
wrongExplanations: LIFO isn't permitted under IFRS reporting and distorts balance-sheet values.
Choosing rates by desired profit IS misrepresentation — the one unforgivable direction in accounting.
Frozen old prices ignore reality and misstate every month after prices move.

questions.scenario: Monsoon leakage damages 300 pcs in the FG store (cost ৳400/pc). Correct treatment:
options: Nothing — damaged goods still count as sellable inventory
Write-down: remove their cost from Inventory through a documented loss entry with approval and disposal evidence
Expense them as COGS — they're gone like a sale
Charge them to H&M's account
questions.explanation: Inventory must be stated at what it can really deliver. Damage write-downs need documents (photos, survey, disposal note) per Module 0's Golden Rule — no document, no entry.
wrongExplanations: Keeping rotten stock valued as good overstates assets AND future COGS.
COGS requires a SALE — damage is a different event with a different account (inventory loss).
H&M never received these pieces; buyers aren't responsible for factory leaks.

questions.scenario: An auditor asks Rafiq: 'Show me what supports April's COGS figure.' A correct perpetual system answers via:
options: An estimate memo from the merchandising team
Shipment-by-shipment drill-down: each B/L-linked entry tracing to lot layers, quantities, and unit costs — every line tied to source documents
Last year's percentage applied to sales
The MD's signature alone
questions.explanation: Perpetual + document-traceability means COGS decomposes into real shipments with real lot costs. That walkable chain (Module 4's rule-version trail) is what makes audits boring — the highest compliment.
wrongExplanations: Estimates have no document lineage; auditors reject them instantly.
Historical ratios can sanity-CHECK figures but never SUBstantiate them.
Signatures support approvals, not arithmetic.

questions.scenario: 500 pcs fail QC BEFORE shipment and get reworked. Separately, AFTER shipment, H&M claims 200 pcs defective. Which statement is right?
options: Both cases are identical COGS adjustments
Pre-shipment rework stays inside production/inventory flows; post-shipment claims touch revenue/AR and possibly reverse COGS for claimed units — different documents, different entries
Both should hit admin expenses
Neither affects accounts
questions.explanation: The ownership line changes everything: before B/L you're fixing your own inventory; after B/L you're settling a commercial dispute with documents (credit notes, claims). Module 13 explores the full messiness.
wrongExplanations: They differ by the most important line in this module — ownership passage.
Neither belongs in admin; one is manufacturing flow, the other is trade settlement.
Ignoring either quietly corrupts inventory value and buyer balances.

questions.scenario: Why does Nasrin's team treating B/L collection casually threaten the P&L?
options: B/Ls only matter for port storage fees
Because the B/L date decides WHEN crores of revenue and COGS land; missing documents shift entire shipments into wrong months, corrupting every trend and covenant check
It doesn't — accounting fixes dates later
Only the bank cares about B/Ls
questions.explanation: Revenue recognition follows documents. A late-collected B/L doesn't change business reality — but it moves reported reality across month boundaries, which lenders, boards, and bonuses all read.
wrongExplanations: Demurrage is real but trivial next to recognition timing.
Backdating or 'fixing later' is falsification, not correction.
Banks care — but your P&L readers care more.

questions.scenario: Which design choice keeps Masco's COGS permanently honest in the ERP?
options: COGS posted from estimated percentages monthly
COGS computed ONLY at shipment from actual consumed lot layers (perpetual), with R4+R5 atomic and negative-stock prevention blocking impossible shipments
COGS entered manually by whichever clerk is free
COGS copied from the buyer's payment amount
questions.explanation: Actual-lot perpetual costing + atomic matching + feasibility guards means every taka of COGS traces to specific shirts that physically left on a specific B/L. Estimates and manual entries reintroduce every lie this module banned.
wrongExplanations: Percentages are the industrialized version of the March/April lie.
Manual COGS invites typos, shortcuts, and 'convenient' months.
Payment amounts include freight terms, FX movement and timing effects — they are NOT product cost.
